explanations.answer: He asks why Balaam didn't come sooner
explanations.explanation: Balak, king of Moab, skips the hello. He goes straight to, “Did I not send you an urgent summons? Why did you not come to me?” (Numbers 22:37). That's a man who sent the invitation, got no quick answer, and drove out to the border himself. I know that feeling. I once waited on a batch that was late, and my mustache did the pacing.

explanations.answer: He thanks Balaam for the long trip
explanations.explanation: No thank-you from Balak. No welcome mat, no "how was the road." The first thing out of his mouth is a question about why Balaam didn't come to him sooner (Numbers 22:37). I think Balak had a lot on his mind.

explanations.answer: He asks Balaam to bless his kingdom
explanations.explanation: A blessing is the opposite of what Balak wants. He is after a curse, and in his oracle Balaam repeats Balak's words: “Come… put a curse on Jacob for me” (Numbers 23:7). At the border, though, the first thing Balak says is a question about why Balaam didn't come. It's a complaint with a crown on.

explanations.answer: Speak only the word God gives him
explanations.explanation: Balaam, the man Balak sent for, doesn't blink. He says, “…I must speak only the word that God puts in my mouth.” (Numbers 22:38). The king had just talked about rewards, and Balaam answers with who he answers to. Friend, that's a short sentence with a lot of weight in it.

explanations.answer: Speak only once he has been paid
explanations.explanation: Balak had just talked about rewarding him richly (Numbers 22:37). Balaam's answer isn't about payment at all. He says he must speak only the word God puts in his mouth. The money talk gets no reply.

explanations.answer: Speak only to the king in private
explanations.explanation: Privacy never comes up. Balaam's words here are about what he is allowed to say, not who hears it. And when his oracle comes, Balak stands there with all the princes of Moab (Numbers 23:6). Nobody is getting a quiet room.
From Bamoth-baal, “he could see the outskirts of the camp of the people.” (Numbers 22:41). Not the middle, just the edge. Think of seeing the parking lot of a bakery, not the ovens.

explanations.answer: The walls of the city of Jericho
explanations.explanation: Jericho never shows up anywhere in this passage. The text says what Balaam could see from there, and it's the outskirts of the camp of the people (Numbers 22:41). I wish I'd had a view like that from my old counter, but all I had was a toaster.

The view is much smaller than that. The text says only the outskirts of the camp of the people (Numbers 22:41). Balak even says later, “You will only see the outskirts of their camp—not all of them.” (Numbers 23:13). So nobody is looking at a whole land from up there.

The text says the opposite. “So Balak did as Balaam had instructed” (Numbers 23:2). The king of Moab doesn't push back or haggle over the altars. He builds them, and then he and Balaam offer a bull and a ram on each one.

Right, and here's what the text says. “So Balak did as Balaam had instructed” (Numbers 23:2). Seven altars is a big job, and Balak goes straight to it. If a customer asked me for that many cookie boxes with no complaint, I'd frame the order.

explanations.answer: That the LORD will meet with him
explanations.explanation: Balaam says, “Perhaps the LORD will meet with me.” (Numbers 23:3). He's hoping for a meeting with God, not a meeting with Balak's wishes. And he adds that whatever the LORD reveals to him, he will tell the king.

explanations.answer: That Israel will move its camp
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing about Israel's camp moving. Balaam's hope in that moment is about the LORD: “Perhaps the LORD will meet with me.” (Numbers 23:3). The camp stays right where it is.

explanations.answer: That Balak will add more silver
explanations.explanation: Silver isn't part of Balaam's hope here. Balaam says, “Perhaps the LORD will meet with me.” (Numbers 23:3). Balak did talk about rewarding him richly earlier (Numbers 22:37), but that's not what Balaam is waiting on up on that height.

Yes, a message. The text says, “Then the LORD put a message in Balaam’s mouth, saying, ‘Return to Balak and give him this message.’” (Numbers 23:5). Balaam isn't making this up as he goes. He's carrying what he was given, and I know what it's like to deliver a box exactly as packed.

A curse is what Balak is hoping for. It isn't what the LORD puts in Balaam's mouth. The text says the LORD put a message there and sent him back to Balak (Numbers 23:5). That message is about to surprise the king.

No riddles here. The word in the text is a message, and it's a message for Balak: “Return to Balak and give him this message.” (Numbers 23:5). The king will understand it just fine, even if he doesn't like it.

It's God. Balaam asks, “How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?” (Numbers 23:8). He doesn't say he won't curse them or that he's too busy. He says the one who decides hasn't cursed them, so he has nothing to say.

Balak is the one asking for a curse, not the one who gets to decide it. Balaam says, “How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?” (Numbers 23:8). The king wants one thing, and Balaam points to who has the final word.

Moab is the king's own country, and its king is the one asking for the curse. Balaam doesn't mention Moab's word in that line at all. He says, “How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?” (Numbers 23:8).

True. Balaam asks, “Who can count the dust of Jacob or number even a fourth of Israel?” (Numbers 23:10). That's a lot of people, friend. I once tried to count sprinkles, and I lost track somewhere around hello.

The text says otherwise. Balaam asks, “Who can count the dust of Jacob or number even a fourth of Israel?” (Numbers 23:10). He says not even a fourth of them can be counted. That's a big crowd, even from the edge.

explanations.answer: To die the death of the righteous
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Balaam says, “Let me die the death of the righteous; let my end be like theirs!” (Numbers 23:10). He has just been looking at Israel, and that's the wish that comes out. I think that's a surprising thing for a man to say with the king of Moab standing right there.

explanations.answer: To be paid the reward of a king
explanations.explanation: Balak did talk about rewarding Balaam richly (Numbers 22:37), but that isn't the wish that ends this oracle. Balaam says, “Let me die the death of the righteous; let my end be like theirs!” (Numbers 23:10). It's a wish for his end, not for a payday.

explanations.answer: To go home to Aram in peace
explanations.explanation: Aram only comes up as the place Balak brought him from (Numbers 23:7). Balaam's closing wish isn't about traveling at all. He says, “Let me die the death of the righteous; let my end be like theirs!” (Numbers 23:10).

Balak says it plainly: “I brought you here to curse my enemies, and behold, you have only blessed them!” (Numbers 23:11). Notice the word only. He didn't get one curse mixed in, he got a blessing the whole way through. I think that's the longest face a king has ever made.
Balak never says warned. His complaint is, “…you have only blessed them!” (Numbers 23:11). He asked for a curse and heard a blessing, and that's what he's upset about.
Balaam did ask who could count Israel (Numbers 23:10), but counting isn't Balak's complaint. He says, “…you have only blessed them!” (Numbers 23:11). So the king heard a blessing, not a head count.
The text says Balak took him “to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah” (Numbers 23:14). New spot, same plan. The king is hoping a different view will give him a different answer.

Carmel isn't named in this passage. The text says Balak took Balaam “to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah” (Numbers 23:14). If you picked a mountain, you were in the right neighborhood of thinking, just the wrong peak.

Hermon doesn't appear in this passage. The text says Balak took Balaam “to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah” (Numbers 23:14). Balak is changing the scenery, so it's easy to mix up the mountains.
Balak asks, “What did the LORD say?” (Numbers 23:17). This time he's the one asking for the message. After round one, I think he already suspects what's coming.
Balak doesn't ask where Balaam has been. He asks, “What did the LORD say?” (Numbers 23:17). He knows Balaam was off meeting the LORD, so it's the message that matters to him.

That question was for the border, back at the start, when Balak said, “Why did you not come to me?” (Numbers 22:37). This time he asks, “What did the LORD say?” (Numbers 23:17). It's a different mood. He's more worried about the message than the clock.

explanations.answer: God does not lie or change His mind
explanations.explanation: That's his point exactly. Balaam says, “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind.” (Numbers 23:19). He follows it with two questions: “Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill?” Balak had been hoping a new mountain might change the answer, and Balaam says it won't.

explanations.answer: God cannot be seen by any people
explanations.explanation: Balaam isn't talking about seeing God here. His point is about God's word: “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind.” (Numbers 23:19). That's a promise about God's character, not a rule about eyes.

explanations.answer: God only speaks through His prophets
explanations.explanation: Balaam doesn't say that in this line. His point is that God is not a man who lies or changes His mind (Numbers 23:19). He's telling Balak that what God says will stand.

He says, “I have indeed received a command to bless; He has blessed, and I cannot change it.” (Numbers 23:20). That follows right after he said God does not change His mind. Balaam isn't the one holding the dial.

Buying it back isn't on the table. Balaam says, “I have indeed received a command to bless; He has blessed, and I cannot change it.” (Numbers 23:20). The king of Moab has offered plenty of talk about rewards, but this isn't a store return.

explanations.answer: It runs out after a year
explanations.explanation: Balaam gives no expiration date. He says, “He has blessed, and I cannot change it.” (Numbers 23:20). Just before that he says, “Does He promise and not fulfill?” (Numbers 23:19). I'd keep my coupons away from this one, since they're the ones with dates.

Balaam says, “God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox.” (Numbers 23:22). So in the middle of this oracle he points back to where Israel came from. It's the strength of God that brought them out.
Babylon isn't named in Balaam's words here. He says, “God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox.” (Numbers 23:22). Egypt is the place he points to.
Assyria doesn't appear in this passage. Balaam says, “God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox.” (Numbers 23:22). It's Egypt he names.

The text says the opposite. Balaam says, “For there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel.” (Numbers 23:23). No right spell, no secret trick. Balak was shopping for one, and that shelf is empty.

Here's what the text says: “For there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel.” (Numbers 23:23). That means no spell works, not even a good one. The king is out of options on that front.

explanations.answer: Only after they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain
explanations.explanation: That's how Balaam's picture ends: “not resting until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain.” (Numbers 23:24). The lion image is about a people who keep going once they rise. It's a picture, and the rest in it comes only at the end.

explanations.answer: Only after the sun goes down and the night grows still
explanations.explanation: Balaam gives no time of day. He says the people don't rest “until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain.” (Numbers 23:24). That's what ends the rest in the picture, not the sunset.

explanations.answer: Only after they find a den high up in the hills
explanations.explanation: There's no den in Balaam's picture. He says they rise like a lioness and do not rest “until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain.” (Numbers 23:24). The hills show up in other lines, but not as a resting place.

True. Balak says, “Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!” (Numbers 23:25). He started out asking for a curse, and now he'll settle for silence. That's the king of Moab going from a big order to just wanting the noise to stop.

The text says Balak does tell him that: “Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!” (Numbers 23:25). He's asking for nothing at all, not a curse and not a blessing. After two blessings, I think he'd take a quiet mountain.

explanations.answer: That God will allow a curse from there
explanations.explanation: Balak says, “Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there.” (Numbers 23:27). He's hoping God might let a curse happen if the spot is different. I think the king is trying a new view for the third time and hoping for a different answer.

explanations.answer: That Israel will move out of sight
explanations.explanation: Israel moving isn't what Balak says he hopes for. He says, “Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there.” (Numbers 23:27). His hope is about the curse, not the camp.

explanations.answer: That Balaam will change his own mind
explanations.explanation: Balak doesn't say that. He says, “Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there.” (Numbers 23:27). Balaam has already told him twice that he speaks what the LORD puts in his mouth.

The text says, “And Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28). That's spot number three. Balak is now running through mountaintops like a man checking every drawer for his keys.
Tabor isn't named in this passage. The text says Balak took Balaam “to the top of Peor” (Numbers 23:28). Three mountains in a row can blur together, I'll give you that.
Gilboa doesn't show up here. The text says Balak took Balaam “to the top of Peor” (Numbers 23:28). Balak keeps moving, so the names are easy to swap.
The text says Peor “overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28). It's a wide, empty view. Balak has gone from one lookout to another, and now he's staring at a whole lot of nothing.
The Jordan River isn't mentioned here. The text says Peor “overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28).
The Salt Sea isn't named in this passage. The text says Peor “overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28). That's the view Balak picked for round three.
